overview.description: Dubbelkingen (Double King) is the premier Flemish variation of the European compendium game known as King. Played primarily in Belgium, it is an marathon trick-taking game consisting of 20 distinct deals. The first half of the game focuses on 'Negative' contracts where players must avoid specific cards or tricks to sidestep penalty points, while the second half switches to 'Positive' contracts where players bid and seek to win tricks. Dubbelkingen adds a strategic layer by allowing players to choose their contracts based on their hand strength, rather than following a fixed sequence.

history.origins: King games are popular across Europe (resembling Barbu), but the Belgian 'Kingen' developed a specific scoring system in the early 20th century. 'Dubbelkingen' was created for serious players who felt the standard 10nddeal game was too reliant on the luck of the deal.
timeline: 1920s: Kingen becomes a staple of Flemish cafe culture.
1950s: Dubbelkingen variant stabilizes with 20 deals (5 per player).
Modern Era: Popularized by the International World Whist Association (IWWA) through tournaments.
history.evolution: Transitions from a fixed-order penalty game to a strategic contract-selection game similar to Bridge or Skat.
history.cultural: Commonly played in 'Volksspelen' (traditional games) gatherings in Ghent and Antwerp.

setup.equipment: 52ndcard deck, complex score sheet for 20 deals.
setup.dealing: Each player receives 13 cards. Dealing is usually done in batches (4-4nd5).

rules.objective: Finish the 20nddeal series with the highest positive score. Negative points from early rounds are offset by positive points from later rounds.
rules.gameplay:
Each of the 4 players must eventually play 5 'contracts' (3 negative, 2 positive):
1. Negative Deals (No Trumps): Avoid taking any tricks, or specific cards like Hearts, Queens, or the King of Hearts.
2. Positive Deals (Trumps): The dealer chooses the trump suit and tries to win as many tricks as possible.
3. Turn Order: Standard Whist-style play. You must follow suit if possible.
keyRules: The Lead: In 'No Hearts' rounds, you cannot lead a Heart until it has been 'broken' (discarded on another suit).
Double Penalty: If a player takes all penalty cards in a round, the penalty often doubles for that player.
Choice: The current dealer chooses which of their 5 contracts to play after looking at their hand.

strategy.basic: In negative rounds, hold onto your small cards (2s, 3s) to ensure you can stay under high cards played by opponents.
strategy.intermediate: Contract Selection: If you have a balanced hand with no long suits, play your 'No Tricks' negative contract early. Save your 'Trumps' positive contract for when you hold an Ace and many cards of one suit.
strategy.advanced: Bleeding the King: If playing 'No King of Hearts,' lead small Hearts early to force the King out while you still have a low card to play underneath it.
tips: Keep track of the Queens! They are highndpenalty cards and can be dumped on any suit once a player is void.
In trump rounds, the dealer has a huge advantage; maximize your score to dig out of your negative hole.

difficulty.easy: Fails to save low cards for negative rounds; picks the wrong contract for its hand.
difficulty.medium: Reasonable 'throwing off' of penalty cards; basic trump management.
difficulty.hard: Expert at 'King of Hearts' trap-laying; perfectly calculates which contract to burn based on the current score delta.

considerations: AI must maintain a longndterm memory of the 20nddeal state to optimize contract selection.

engine.deckDescription: A standard 52-card French deck comprising four suits: Hearts, Diamonds, Clubs, and Spades. Each suit contains thirteen ranks: Ace, 2 through 10, Jack, Queen, and King, providing versatile options for various card games.
engine.suitDescription: Four traditional French suits: Hearts (Cœur), Diamonds (Carreau), Clubs (Trèfle), and Spades (Pique), each represented with standard French card iconography and distinct color coding for easy identification.
engine.rankDescription: Standard thirteen ranks per suit: Ace, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, Jack, Queen, and King, where each rank has distinct value and meaning depending on the specific game rules and player strategies.
